description_full: Kenon Holdings Ltd., through its subsidiaries, operates as an owner, developer, and operator of power generation facilities in Israel and the United States. It engages in the generation and supply of electricity, and energy; development, construction, operation of power plants, and energy generation facilities using natural gas and renewable energy; and management of solar and wind energy, and conventional natural gas-fired power plants. The company was incorporated in 2014 and is based in Singapore. Kenon Holdings Ltd. is a subsidiary of Ansonia Holdings Singapore B.V.

financial_summary: Kenon Holdings Ltd. is a mid-cap utilities business with a $3.2B market cap on $872M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 2% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 19% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $167M in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.91× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Net dilution runs at 8.1% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 63% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin trails the Utilities median (21%) by 14pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.37x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.0% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-10.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 16% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 8% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 37% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 0.83, it moves roughly with the market.
Trading is thin (about $887K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 52% in the 2020 crash and 42% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 72% below its DCF fair value of $218, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $82.67 to $508 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Utilities peers: P/E 26.6 vs 20.3 and EV/EBITDA 35.4 vs 12.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 143% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 6.7% annual cash-flow growth, 18pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.08).
It runs a 19% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.91x.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.8x net debt to EBITDA ($1.5B of cash against $1.7B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 15.0% over 3 years and 17.7% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 1.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 56.7% a year over five years.
own: Insiders own 62.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 25%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-8.1%), diluting holders.
It pays out 168% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 354 employees, each generates about $2.5M of revenue, 2.4x the Utilities median, and revenue has grown 11.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $473K of free cash flow per employee.
